paragraphs.text: Last month the city council debated whether to make the 14 and 22 bus lines free for riders. Supporters packed the meeting, and so did a few business owners who were worried about the cost. This essay will look at both sides of the free-bus debate. I take the 22 to campus every morning, so I have seen who rides it and who does not. Most mornings the bus is full before it reaches the hospital stop.

paragraphs.text: Fares are a bigger barrier than most people think, a monthly pass costs $64, which is more than many students spend on food in a week. A pass is cheaper per ride than single fares, but only if you can pay $64 at once. My roommate walks forty minutes to her job to save the fare, and some weeks she cannot afford the pass at all. When Riverton made its buses free two years ago, ridership went up. People who had stopped riding came back, especially older residents and part-time workers. Free fares would also save drivers the time they spend making change.

paragraphs.text: The main objection is cost. Fares pay for about a fifth of the system, and the city would have to replace that money from somewhere. This is a fair point, and I understand why people worry about it. Some council members said a small fee keeps riders respectful, I do not think that is true. Most of the people I see on the 22 are tired, not rude.

paragraphs.text: Free buses would also help the environment. More riders means fewer cars downtown and less traffic near the hospital, where ambulances get stuck every afternoon. On my route I count at least ten cars for every bus at the Grant Street light. The council's own report says the downtown streets are already over capacity at rush hour. Cleaner air matters to everyone who lives near Grant Street. Buses would get crowded, but the city could add more.

If ridership grows the way it did in Riverton, the council will have its answer.

item.text: Your conclusion already gives the council a specific proposal: a one-year trial on the 14 and 22. I’ll save a checklist that starts there and gives you time after work to tackle the Riverton evidence and the funding objection. I’ll also flag three grammar fixes for you to review.

items.text: Start with your one-year trial (10 min). In paragraph 1, move the proposal you already wrote for the 14 and 22 into the spot where you announce the debate. Which detail from your ride or your roommate’s walk best explains why you want the council to try it? Give that reason in your own words.

Check Riverton (25 min). Find the source you used for the ridership claim. Record who published it, what dates it compares, and the size of the change. Explain what that comparison tells you about the proposed trial. If the source gives no figures or rider breakdown, narrow your claim to what you can verify.

Answer the cost question in paragraph 3 (30 min). Check what the one-fifth figure covers. Use the council’s budget or meeting record to identify a funding option for the two routes. Explain what it could cover and what trade-off it would involve. If you keep the separate point about “respectful” riders, check who said it and what they meant.

Give paragraph 4 one job (20 min). If you keep the traffic point, explain how removing fares would change trips at Grant Street. What evidence shows that some new riders would otherwise drive? Revisit the last line about crowding. Develop it using your observation at the hospital stop and consider the cost, or cut it.

Return to the trial in your conclusion (15 min). Once the proposal is in the introduction, use the ending to explain what the council should look for after a year and how that would answer the concerns you discussed. The draft is 391 words and the target is about 1,000. Give most of the extra space to your evidence and your answer on funding.

Proofread and submit (15 min). Review the two comma-splice suggestions and the verb after “More riders.” Check any new sentences for the same patterns, confirm your sources and word count, then submit your chosen version by 11:59 p.m.

paragraphs.text: Last month the city council debated whether to make the 14 and 22 bus lines free for riders. Supporters packed the meeting, and so did a few business owners who were worried about the cost. This essay will look at both sides of the free-bus debate. I take the 22 to campus every morning, so I have seen who rides it and who does not. Most mornings the bus is full before it reaches the hospital stop.

paragraphs.text: Fares are a bigger barrier than most people think, a monthly pass costs $64, which is more than many students spend on food in a week. A pass is cheaper per ride than single fares, but only if you can pay $64 at once. My roommate walks forty minutes to her job to save the fare, and some weeks she cannot afford the pass at all. When Riverton made its buses free two years ago, ridership went up. People who had stopped riding came back, especially older residents and part-time workers. Free fares would also save drivers the time they spend making change.

paragraphs.text: The main objection is cost. Fares pay for about a fifth of the system, and the city would have to replace that money from somewhere. This is a fair point, and I understand why people worry about it. Some council members said a small fee keeps riders respectful, I do not think that is true. Most of the people I see on the 22 are tired, not rude.

paragraphs.text: Free buses would also help the environment. More riders means fewer cars downtown and less traffic near the hospital, where ambulances get stuck every afternoon. On my route I count at least ten cars for every bus at the Grant Street light. The council's own report says the downtown streets are already over capacity at rush hour. Cleaner air matters to everyone who lives near Grant Street. Buses would get crowded, but the city could add more.

items.text: Start with your one-year trial (10 min). In paragraph 1, move the proposal you already wrote for the 14 and 22 into the spot where you announce the debate. Which detail from your ride or your roommate’s walk best explains why you want the council to try it? Give that reason in your own words.

Check Riverton (25 min). Find the source you used for the ridership claim. Record who published it, what dates it compares, and the size of the change. Explain what that comparison tells you about the proposed trial. If the source gives no figures or rider breakdown, narrow your claim to what you can verify.

Answer the cost question in paragraph 3 (30 min). Check what the one-fifth figure covers. Use the council’s budget or meeting record to identify a funding option for the two routes. Explain what it could cover and what trade-off it would involve. If you keep the separate point about “respectful” riders, check who said it and what they meant.

Give paragraph 4 one job (20 min). If you keep the traffic point, explain how removing fares would change trips at Grant Street. What evidence shows that some new riders would otherwise drive? Revisit the last line about crowding. Develop it using your observation at the hospital stop and consider the cost, or cut it.

Return to the trial in your conclusion (15 min). Once the proposal is in the introduction, use the ending to explain what the council should look for after a year and how that would answer the concerns you discussed. The draft is 391 words and the target is about 1,000. Give most of the extra space to your evidence and your answer on funding.

Proofread and submit (15 min). Review the two comma-splice suggestions and the verb after “More riders.” Check any new sentences for the same patterns, confirm your sources and word count, then submit your chosen version by 11:59 p.m.

When you get off work at nine, start with the proposal you already wrote in your conclusion. Move the one-year trial on routes 14 and 22 into your introduction and explain why you support it. Then spend most of your writing time on two questions: How much did ridership change in Riverton, according to which source? How would the city cover lost fares during the trial?

Your draft is 391 words, and the final calls for about 1,000. The checklist budgets just under two hours for revision, proofreading, and submission. You’ll need to submit your final version by 11:59 p.m. tonight.
